{{Group theory sidebar}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''semitopological group''' is a [[topological space]] with a [[Group (mathematics)|group operation]] that is [[Continuous function#Continuous functions between topological spaces|continuous]] with respect to each variable considered separately. It is a weakening of the concept of a [[topological group]]; all topological groups are semitopological groups but the [[Converse (logic)|converse]] does not hold.

==Formal definition==
A semitopological group <math>G</math> is a topological space that is also a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] such that

:<math>g_1: G \times G \to G : (x,y)\mapsto xy</math>

is continuous with respect to both <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. (Note that a topological group is continuous with reference to both variables simultaneously, and <math>g_2: G\to G : x \mapsto x^{-1}</math> is also required to be continuous. Here <math> G \times G </math> is viewed as a topological space with the [[product topology]].)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Husain|first1=Taqdir|title=Introduction to Topological Groups|date=2018|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|isbn=9780486828206|pages=27|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7YJIDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA27|language=en}}</ref>

Clearly, every topological group is a semitopological group. To see that the converse does not hold, consider the [[real line]] <math>(\mathbb{R},+)</math> with its usual structure as an additive [[abelian group]]. Apply the [[lower limit topology]] to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with [[topological basis]] the family <math>\{[a,b):-\infty < a < b < \infty \}</math>. Then <math>g_1</math> is continuous, but <math>g_2</math> is not continuous at 0: <math>[0,b)</math> is an [[open neighbourhood]] of 0 but there is no neighbourhood of 0 contained in <math>g_2^{-1}([0,b))</math>.

It is known that any [[locally compact]] Hausdorff semitopological group is a topological group.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Arhangel’skii|first1=Alexander|author-link=Alexander Arhangelskii|last2=Tkachenko|first2=Mikhail|title=Topological Groups and Related Structures, An Introduction to Topological Algebra.|date=2008|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9789491216350|pages=114|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hIEnzrOBbW0C&pg=PA114|language=en}}</ref> Other similar results are also known.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Aull|first1=C. E.|last2=Lowen|first2=R.|title=Handbook of the History of General Topology|date=2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9789401704700|pages=1119|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eILrCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA1119|language=en}}</ref>
